analysis.one_liner: Requires federal contractors to pay workers at least $7.50 an hour or a family-of-four poverty wage.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in two House committees for the full two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require companies holding federal contracts worth more than $10,000 to pay every worker on that contract the greater of $7.50 an hour or the hourly wage needed for a full-time worker to reach the federal poverty line for a family of four. Small businesses were exempt, as were nonprofits whose CEOs earn no more than 25 times their lowest-paid worker. Companies that violated it would lose their federal contracts and be barred from new ones for five years, and would owe workers back pay plus equal damages.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers on federal contracts who earned less than $7.50 an hour — the federal minimum wage was $5.15 at the time — in jobs like janitorial work, food service, and building services. The bill also banned firing workers to replace them with cheaper trainees.

how_it_helps.text: Covered federal contractors and subcontractors must pay each worker the greater of $7.50 an hour or the hourly wage needed, working 40 hours a week, to reach the federal poverty level for a family of four.

Employers who underpay workers would have their contracts suspended, be barred from federal contracting for five years, and owe workers their unpaid wages plus an equal amount in damages, paid out by the Labor Department.
The bill prohibits employers from laying off a covered worker and replacing them with a trainee or apprentice who does not qualify for the higher wage.

The bill's findings state the federal government spends billions of dollars a year subsidizing businesses through contracts and the tax code, arguing taxpayers' money should improve workers' economic security.

analysis.who_pays: Federal contractors employing low-wage workers, who would see their labor costs rise; those costs could partly flow into federal contract prices and ultimately to taxpayers. Small businesses and most nonprofits were carved out.

drawbacks.text: The wage mandate raised covered contractors' labor costs, and economists generally expect some of that cost to be passed to the government in contract prices — meaning taxpayers would help fund the raise.

The five-year debarment penalty was strict by contracting standards, and critics of contractor living-wage rules argue such mandates shrink opportunities for the least-experienced workers or push firms toward the small-business exemption.
The bill covered only workers on federal contracts, leaving out low-wage workers whose employers hold no federal business.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a direct, enforceable raise to low-wage workers whose wages were already being paid with federal dollars, with a real enforcement mechanism in back pay, damages, and debarment. Its costs fell mainly on contractors and, indirectly, on federal contract budgets. Its main limitation was its narrow reach: it touched only contract workers, not the broader low-wage workforce.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees in the first weeks of 1997, and no committee ever acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Luis Gutierrez introduced the bill on January 7, 1997, the first day of the 105th Congress.
The House referred it to both the Education and the Workforce Committee and the Government Reform and Oversight Committee on the day it was introduced.
Within its first month it was sent to the Subcommittee on Government Management, Information and Technology and the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, and no further action was ever recorded.
The bill ended the Congress with no hearing, no markup, and no vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal contractors employing low-wage workers were better off, since they continued paying the $5.15 federal minimum wage with no new wage floor, damages exposure, or debarment risk. The 27-member coalition behind the bill gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Luis Gutierrez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Federal Living Wage Responsibility Act on the first day of the 105th Congress.

for.name: 27 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 27 were Democrats or the chamber's independent.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on January 7, 1997, sent it to its Workforce Protections subcommittee on January 31, and never reported it or held a vote.

against.name: House Committee on Government Reform and Oversight
against.what_they_did: Received the bill the day it was introduced, sent it to its Government Management subcommittee on January 16, and never acted further.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Controlled the committees and floor schedule throughout the 105th Congress; neither the committees nor the leadership ever brought the bill forward.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes were ever taken; sponsorship was entirely Democratic and independent, while the Republican majority controlled the committees where the bill sat untouched.

industries.industry: Federal contractors employing low-wage workers (janitorial, food service, building services)
industries.note: These firms would have had to raise wages from the then-$5.15 federal minimum to $7.50 or more for contract workers, and faced suspension, five-year debarment, and double damages for violations. Their continued ability to pay minimum wage on taxpayer-funded contracts depended on the bill never moving.
The bill exempted small business concerns from the wage requirement, giving them a cost advantage over large covered contractors, though the bill imposed nothing on them.
Nonprofits were exempt unless their CEO earned more than 25 times their lowest-paid full-time-equivalent worker, so high-pay nonprofits would have been covered while others were not.
